summary: The note describes 'Empty Nest Syndrome', the sadness, loneliness and loss of identity many parents feel when their children leave home, through several couples and individuals who became empty nesters in autumn 2023. It covers emotional swings, strain on relationships, and coping strategies recommended by psychologist Dr. Elizabeth Kingston, such as new routines, hobbies, volunteering, travel and counseling. It concludes that the transition can become a time of rediscovery and a full life.
one_line: Parents who became empty nesters in 2023 describe loneliness, identity shifts and ways of coping, from hobbies and volunteering to counseling.
key_facts: Empty nest syndrome is not an officially recognized medical condition but is widely acknowledged as a transitional period that can cause sadness and loss of purpose.

Dr. Elizabeth Kingston, a psychologist specializing in family dynamics, defines it as "a psychological condition that affects primarily those who find their identity strongly linked with their role as a caregiver."
Janet and David Thompson of suburban Cleveland have lived in a silent house since September 5, 2023, after nearly three decades of raising three children.
George Martinez of Atlanta became an empty nester in December 2023 when his last child left, and said he had to figure out who George was all over again.
Susan Grant of Portland felt an emotional rollercoaster after her daughter left for college on September 12, 2023.
Mary and Bob Spencer became empty nesters on September 20, 2023 when their twin sons went to different universities, and within weeks felt profound loneliness.
Sarah and Jim Reynolds, empty nesters since November 3, 2023, are working to maintain a healthy marriage and learn to be 'us' again, not just mom and dad.
Dr. Kingston advises establishing new routines, rediscovering old passions or exploring new ones, staying connected with others and communicating feelings.
Bill and Anne Clarkson, empty nesters since September 15, 2023, took up traveling, which Anne called like a second honeymoon.
Natalie Turner began volunteering at her local library in October 2023 to connect with others and gain purpose.
Jack Robinson turned the spare bedroom into a woodworking shop after his daughter moved out in late September 2023.
Laura and Kevin Bates, empty nesters since October 8, 2023, found couples counseling helpful for communicating and supporting each other.
